A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GameGen-X and OGameData study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison across relocations and renumbering. The embedded Figure 1 video is identical.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation and control evaluations, component ablations in Tables 2–5, dataset analyses and qualitative experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a dataset/model contribution comparison and generation speed–quality experiments in Tables 7, 10 and 11.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same foundation model, masking procedure, frozen-backbone instruction tuning and multimodal InstructNet control. New Appendix C documents architecture and training details without establishing a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: Coverage remains open-world game generation and character/environment control using OGameData and game-domain MiraData. The OGameEval generation and control benchmarks are retained. Clarified data sources and the additional contribution and speed analyses do not establish new represented tasks or populations.

E2.justification: New Table 7 adds OpenSora trained on OGameData to the dataset/model contribution comparison. The original generation, control and commercial comparator sets remain unchanged. v2 explains Mira's absence from Table 3; it was already absent in v1.

E3.justification: The added analyses introduce stated 10K training subsets, a 30-inference speed protocol on A800/H800 GPUs, resolution and sampling-step sweeps, and additional and aggregate quality metrics (D.1, D.4). The retained ablation hardware statement changes from eight H100 to eight H800 GPUs; this reported revision does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled comparison intended to separate dataset and architecture contributions (Table 7), plus quantitative and qualitative analyses of generation speed and sensitivity to resolution and sampling steps (Tables 10–11, Figures 16–17). The original component and data-strategy ablations remain.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 newly reports three videos generated with different random seeds per control prompt. v1 described expert averaging without this repetition information. This is newly disclosed seed coverage, not an established increase in runs; confidence intervals and variability estimates remain absent.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 retain their scores. New Table 7 reports additional comparisons, including OpenSora/OGameData FID 295.0 and FVD 1186.0. Tables 10–11 and Figures 16–17 add speed–quality findings, including 5.1 seconds for 102 frames at 320×256 with 10 steps on H800. The stated 10K contribution experiment should not be treated as a same-setting rerun of the original 20K generation ablations.

T1.justification: The method's mathematical formulation remains unchanged. Appendix D.1 introduces limited definitions of composite evaluation scores: mean FID/FVD for domain alignment and a mean of six metrics for visual quality; D.4 similarly defines an overall five-metric average. No new theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claims concerning interactive open-world video generation, the million-clip OGameData dataset, two-stage InstructNet training and superior generation/control are retained. The shortened abstract does not materially narrow these contributions, and the introduction retains the 150-plus-game scope.

C2.justification: D.1 adds arguments supporting comparator fairness and attributing benefits separately to the dataset and architecture. D.4 interprets the speed–quality tradeoff and the sampling requirements of higher resolutions. The existing limitations concerning real-time interaction, consistency, physics and complex actions are retained in Appendix E.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies task/control sampling probabilities, preprocessing, optimizer and training duration, architecture dimensions, pseudocode and computational costs. B.1–B.2 add stated YouTube-ID sharing terms and synchronized keyboard/gameplay collection details. D.3 expands evaluator recruitment and scoring documentation. These substantially extend reproducibility information rather than establish a redesigned method.

R1.justification: v2 adds Oasis to the game-simulation discussion and references query-key normalization, RoPE and the Stable Diffusion VAE in its implementation account. It also acknowledges existing video datasets as sources. The principal research positioning remains intact; duplicate T5 and tokenizer references do not represent additional distinct prior works.

P1.justification: The abstract, selected main-text passages and acknowledgments receive limited edits. The appendices gain dedicated implementation, fairness, human-evaluation and speed subsections, with metric explanations rearranged. Most pre-existing prose and its narrative order remain intact; the expansion primarily documents additional technical and experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adds four substantive tables (6, 7, 10 and 11), two sampling-quality figures (16–17) and boxed model pseudocode. Figure 2's graphics are refreshed, and dataset displays and evaluation rubrics are rearranged. The earlier qualitative Figures 16–35 are retained as Figures 18–37, rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses missing reproducibility information through explicit training schedules, architecture dimensions, pseudocode and resource costs. Its speed–quality measurements also make the feasibility of the proposed interactive generation more assessable than v1's qualitative discussion of computational limitations. The new attribution analysis has a prose/table mismatch about OpenSora's dataset and an unclear relationship between its 10K setting and the retained 20K ablations. These weaknesses limit that analysis, but the documentation and feasibility evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
